extracted.intended_audience: NLP and AI researchers, conference organizers (program chairs, meta-reviewers), reviewers, and policymakers interested in machine-assisted peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Mapping the problem space and concrete opportunities for NLP to assist scholarly peer review (particularly conference peer review in AI/NLP), including stages from submission screening through matching, review writing, meta-reviewing, decisions, and post-review analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review goals (gatekeeping, prioritization, feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: At its best, peer review should gate-keep against methodologically flawed research, help prioritize the rest based on novelty and impact, and provide useful feedback to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three functions are presented as the core expectations of scholarly peer review. Systems or policies (including NLP tools) should be judged on whether they help achieve these functions without undermining them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing should be objective, thorough, and impartial
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing should be objective, thorough, and impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a normative standard for reviewers and for systems that assist reviewing; tools and processes should avoid introducing or amplifying subjectivity or bias and aim to support thorough, impartial evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic minimum standard of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: At its realistic minimum, peer review should keep out papers with obvious flaws and help moderate discussion of ongoing work in the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when ideal goals are unattainable at scale, systems should at least help filter out clearly flawed submissions and provide a platform for community discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening: formatting and formal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Screening should ensure correct manuscript formatting (page count, font size, layout and margins), correct display of figures, and formatting of references, and other basic parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet formatting or formal checks can lead to desk rejection. NLP/surface-level tools (e.g., ACL pubcheck) can automate many of these checks to reduce burden on chairs and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening: presence of required content-level sections and checklist consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Screening should detect the presence of required content sections (e.g., limitations, broader ethical impact) and verify that checklist answers correspond to the indicated paper sections (e.g., reproducibility, compensation to human participants, adherence to data licenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple NLP automation can detect whether required sections exist and cross-check checklist answers with the manuscript text to avoid accidental errors and speed up checklist completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening: misconduct and policy-violation detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Screening should detect plagiarism and self-plagiarism, anonymity violations, dual or duplicate submissions, papers from fake paper mills, potentially machine-generated text, and enforce compliance with editorial guidelines on the use of AI for writing assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced screening combines NLP with other methods (e.g., plagiarism detectors, image-manipulation tools) to flag potential policy violations for human inspection prior to or instead of desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript quality metrics (coherence, citation coverage, readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial manuscript quality can be analyzed for coherence, citation coverage, and readability to inform desk-rejection candidates, mentoring needs, reviewer allocation, and post-hoc analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NLP assistance could provide these analyses at screening time to help program chairs identify manuscripts needing mentoring or special handling and to study manuscript quality effects on outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on use of generative AI for writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies that introduce new intellectual content to the paper are not allowed; using NLP systems to improve writing and clarity without altering the intellectual contribution of the manuscript is allowed (e.g., fixing typos, correcting grammar, flagging verbosity/readability/repetition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes adherence to venue norms (e.g., ACL 2023 policy). Allowed functionality includes paraphrasing for style and surface editing; disallowed functionality includes adding scientific ideas or substantive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadata quality: keywords, track, and contribution type
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission metadata (keywords, track, contribution type) is important for matching and program navigation; keywords must be concise yet descriptive and can be hard to select.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NLP-assisted keyword generation and automatic track suggestion can help authors create better metadata. Poor metadata leads to poor reviewer assignment; techniques like imputing fractional keyword scores or using semantic representations can mitigate issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer–paper matching objective: topical overlap, diversity, conflict avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment should aim to maximize topical overlap and diversity of the reviewer set for each manuscript while avoiding conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching algorithms and scoring methods should optimize for expertise alignment and diversity (e.g., methodological perspectives) and respect COI constraints; NLP-derived scores are one input among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise scoring: text-similarity approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive similarity between submission text (title, abstract, full paper) and a candidate reviewer's publication history to score reviewer–paper matches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text-similarity approaches are intuitive (e.g., LDA, encoder-based embeddings, general-purpose paper representations) but face challenges: publication history may not reflect current expertise, similarity can capture irrelevant surface signals, and dense representations can lack interpretability. Evaluations find room for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer–paper scoring: keyword-based matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Match papers and reviewers using manually provided or predicted keywords (area, contribution type, language studied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keywords are more interpretable than dense similarity scores and can increase acceptance for minority contribution types, but poor keyword selection reduces differentiation. NLP can assist in preparing effective keyword lists and mapping related/disambiguated keywords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer interest capture: bidding as a signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Bidding allows reviewers to indicate interest or lack thereof for reviewing specific submissions and is primarily a measure of interest (not necessarily expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bidding can be combined with text-similarity and keyword approaches to present reviewers with a manageable subset to bid on; monitor the number of bids per paper to ensure adequate coverage. Be aware bidders may pursue high-quality or personally beneficial papers rather than pure expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability and explainability of matching scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching scores should be interpretable; keywords provide explanations while dense semantic similarity representations often lack interpretability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dense embeddings are less interpretable, matching systems should include explanation mechanisms or rely on more interpretable signals (keywords, explicit overlap) where trust and transparency are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and reliability of reviewer profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication history and self-reported profiles may be incomplete or inaccurate; matching should account for profile incompleteness and potential miscalibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should treat profile-derived expertise scores with caution and incorporate additional signals (bidding, recent publications, manual curation) or uncertainty modeling when assigning reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review report structure: semi-structured essay, scores and checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reviewer writes a review report: a short semi-structured essay often accompanied by a range of scores (overall score, confidence, soundness, novelty) and checklists (e.g., adherence to ethics guidelines or data availability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review forms combine free-text with structured scores to support meta-reviewing and program-chair decisions. NLP assistance can target both prose (summarization, clarity checks) and structured elements (validating checklist consistency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review responsibilities and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-reviewers write a meta-review report — a brief text that summarizes reviewers' feedback and provides their own evaluation of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-reviews synthesize reviews and can request further reviews when reports are missing/low-quality or when ethical concerns exist. NLP tools could assist by generating drafts, extracting key points, and flagging inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality: thoroughness vs fast-reject heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality reviewing requires informed, well-reasoned reports; low-quality reviewing includes generic, hastily written reviews and the use of fast-reject heuristics like 'not state of the art', 'too niche', or 'writing too bad' instead of thorough evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational measures (reviewer mentoring, training) and NLP tools (scaffolding, checkers) can improve review quality. Systems should detect low-effort reviews and support reviewer development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias mitigation strategies in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation strategies include reviewer and author anonymization and assigning multiple reviewers per submission to reduce prestige/nationality/gender/language/proficiency/confirmation/publication biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are partial remedies and do not fully solve bias; NLP systems that assist decision-making should be evaluated for potential bias amplification and designed with mitigation in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and mitigation of strategic and dishonest behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should detect and mitigate strategic behaviors (e.g., downscoring competitors, collusion rings) and dishonest practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment, monitoring, and post-hoc analysis tools can flag suspicious patterns. NLP methods for anomaly detection and behavioral analysis can help but require careful validation and ethical safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload balancing and assignment capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer workloads (typical 3–6 submissions per reviewer) should be managed to avoid overload and preserve review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment algorithms should consider reviewer capacity and balance load; bidding and matching systems can be designed to account for available reviewing time and to ensure fair distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening for ethical and legal compliance (data licenses, participant compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screening should check for adherence to data licenses, appropriate compensation/ethics for human participants, and other legal/ethical constraints called out in checklists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated checks can surface possible license violations or missing ethics statements for human inspection; accurate detection helps prevent later policy violations and ensures reproducibility claims can be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability and trust in NLP-assisted tools
rubrics_metrics.description: NLP assistance must be trustworthy: users accord low trust to opaque scores and desire interpretable explanations for system outputs (e.g., why a reviewer was matched).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices should prioritize transparency (e.g., showing keyword overlap, example supporting papers) and provide human-controllable overrides, since opaque automated assistance can reduce community trust.
